title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Show me a developer's 10-year cumulative operating cash flow beside its 10-year net profit, and I will tell you whether it is compounding capital or merely rolling inventory.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Principle

web_blocks.html: A twelve-year forensic review (FY15–FY26, plus TTM Sep 2026) shows rapid P&L scale paired with working-capital drag and modest return ratios [8]. Consolidated revenue rose from ₹165 crore in FY15 to a ₹277–382 crore plateau across FY16–FY21 [8]. It then jumped 3.1x from ₹347 crore in FY21 to ₹1,090 crore in FY26 and ₹1,247 crore TTM (Sep 2026) [8][10]. Over FY21–FY26, operating profit tripled from ₹95 crore to ₹299 crore (OPM 27–31%) [8]. Net profit expanded 5.1x from ₹31 crore to ₹157 crore (₹180 crore TTM) [8][10]. Interest expense fell from 63% of operating profit in FY20 (₹66 crore on ₹105 crore EBITDA) to 24% in FY26 (₹73 crore on ₹299 crore EBITDA) [8].

On the balance sheet, total assets more than doubled from ₹1,176 crore in FY15 to ₹2,594 crore in FY26 (₹2,515 crore as of Sep 2026) [8]. 'Other Assets' dominate at ₹2,290 crore as of Sep 2026, reflecting work-in-progress inventory, land, and customer receivables [8]. Borrowings peaked at ₹968 crore in FY20 against ₹638 crore net worth (~1.52x D/E) [8]. Debt then declined to ₹808 crore (FY24), ₹676 crore (FY25), ₹711 crore (FY26), and ₹654 crore in Sep 2026 [8]. Management reports ₹646 crore gross debt and 0.44x D/E [14]. In FY25, a ₹225 crore preferential allotment of 31.64 lakh shares lifted equity capital from ₹35 crore to ₹39 crore and reserves from ₹830 crore to ₹1,167 crore [8][12]. Promoter holding shifted from 74.20% to 68.23% (68.56% by Sep 2026) [8][14]. CRISIL reaffirmed its Crisil A-/Stable rating in August 2025 and August 2026, noting committed receivables cover 100% of balance construction costs [1][25].

Cash Conversion & Forensic Watch-Outs: Despite strong headline PAT growth, 12-year cumulative Operating Cash Flow (FY15–FY26) is only ~₹461 crore [8]. That equals ~53% of ~₹870 crore cumulative net profit over the same period [8]. FY21 (₹201 crore CFO), FY23 (₹135 crore), and FY24 (₹220 crore) delivered strong cash inflows upon project handovers [8]. However, FY25 CFO dropped to ₹8 crore (21% CFO/EBITDA) and FY26 CFO was ₹69 crore (47% CFO/EBITDA vs. ₹157 crore PAT) as new launches absorbed cash [8]. Return ratios also remain modest: 3-year average ROE is 11.9% (TTM ROE 11.5%, ROCE 14.3%) [8]. Working Capital Days stood at 591 days in FY26, with Debtor Days elevated at 142 days [8]. Investors must monitor management's FY27 guidance that D/E could rise back toward 1.0x to fund the Wadala Boutique Office and 8 planned launches [10].

web_blocks.mechanism: Held massive Mumbai land banks and Slum Rehabilitation (SRA) / airport-slum entitlements on paper, but funded slow-moving approvals and working capital with high-cost corporate debt while cash conversion lagged accounting profits.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Debt swelled past ₹7,000+ Cr as project approvals and TDR monetization stalled; interest coverage collapsed, leading to loan defaults and NCLT insolvency admission in 2019 with near-total equity wipeout.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Paper GDV in Mumbai (such as Kanjurmarg) cannot service debt on its own. Ajmera's decision to raise ₹225 Cr equity and cut D/E to 0.44x avoids HDIL's leverage trap—provided management honors its 1.0x gearing ceiling in FY27.

web_blocks.title: Forensic Checklist: Ind AS 115, Dilution & Gearing
paragraphs: 1. Ind AS 115 Lag: Committed sales pending recognition stood at ₹1,550–1,850 Cr in FY26–H1 FY27, providing P&L visibility, but cash flow depends on milestone collections, not accounting recognition [10][14].

2. Equity Dilution: The FY25 preferential issue (₹225 Cr) permanently strengthened net worth to ₹1,467 Cr (Sep 2026) and lowered interest burden, though future SPV-level equity tie-ups for Kanjurmarg could share project upside [8][10].
3. Gearing Watch: Re-leveraging from 0.44x toward 1.0x in FY27 is manageable if pre-sales hit ₹2,200 Cr, but risky if launches slip again [10][14].

book_paragraphs: Now you and I turn to the financial forensics—the part of the audit that separates genuine compounding from accounting optical illusions. If you look solely at Ajmera's income statement from FY21 to FY26, the recovery looks like a textbook turnaround: sales up more than threefold to ₹1,090 crore, operating margins holding a respectable 27% to 31%, and net profit multiplying 5.1 times from ₹31 crore to ₹157 crore (and ₹180 crore on a trailing twelve-month basis through September 2026). Even interest expense, which used to consume over 60% of operating profit in FY20, fell to 24% of operating profit in FY26.

Yet when you flip the page to the cash-flow statement, a more sobering reality emerges. Across the entire twelve-year span from FY15 through FY26, Ajmera generated roughly ₹461 crore in cumulative operating cash flow against ₹870 crore in cumulative net profit—barely 53% cumulative cash conversion. In FY25, net profit was ₹126 crore while operating cash flow was just ₹8 crore; in FY26, net profit was ₹157 crore while operating cash flow was ₹69 crore. Why? Because in growth-mode real estate, every rupee collected from an older tower gets immediately poured into the excavation, steel, and Mivan formwork of the next tower.

That working-capital hunger also explains why Ajmera's return on equity has averaged just 11.9% over the past three years (11.5% trailing) and return on capital employed sits at 14.3%, despite near-zero land cost in Wadala. Over ₹2,290 crore of 'Other Assets'—largely inventory and receivables—sits on the balance sheet, with working capital cycling at nearly 591 days and debtor days at 142 days. The FY25 preferential equity raise of ₹225 crore was a smart move to de-risk the balance sheet and cut debt-to-equity to 0.44x, but with management guiding leverage back toward 1.0x in FY27 to fund the Wadala Boutique Office and eight new launches, cash conversion will be the single most important number to police.

You should also keep an eye on the subtle shift in shareholding and capital structure. Promoter ownership stepped down from 74.20% to 68.23% during the FY25 preferential issue (and ticked up slightly to 68.56% by September 2026), while institutional DII and FII participation remains tiny at under 2% combined. That means Ajmera is still very much a promoter-anchored mid-cap where balance-sheet discipline—specifically keeping net debt inside the 1.0x ceiling—matters far more than short-term earnings beats.

book_callouts.title: Why 11.9% ROE Demands Discipline
book_callouts.text: A business earning 11.5%–14.3% returns on capital cannot afford prolonged idle land like Kanjurmarg or slow-moving luxury inventory in Versova. Asset turns—launching, selling, and collecting quickly—are the only lever that lifts ROE toward 18%+.

book_callouts.title: The 53% Cash-Conversion Reality Check
book_callouts.text: Across twelve years (FY15–FY26), Ajmera converted just 53% of its cumulative accounting profit into operating cash flow. Never value a developer on peak P&L earnings without checking working-capital absorption.

book_subsections.title: The Base-Rate Lesson from Mumbai's Past
paragraphs: Mumbai real estate history is littered with developers who mistook land-bank appraisals for liquidity. HDIL once boasted tens of millions of square feet of Mumbai and SRA rights, yet collapsed into insolvency in 2019 when stalled approvals met high-cost debt.

Ajmera is in a far healthier position today—with 0.44x debt-to-equity, a Crisil A-/Stable rating, and 100% construction-cost coverage from committed receivables—but the HDIL base rate is why you should watch net debt and Kanjurmarg clearances like a hawk.
